segments.description: We welcome Eva Boris to the Grand Slam Coaches Conference. She's a remarkable individual whose journey spans both the world of professional tennis and the realm of sports psychology. As a tennis player, she held an impressive rank of world number 500 on the WTA circuit. However, her passion for the mental aspect of sport led to a distinguished career as a sports psychologist. For 12 years, she was based at the Juan Carlos Ferrero Tennis Academy, Equal Eat in Spain. And later, six years, she served as the performance mental consultant at the Emilio Sanchez Tennis Academy in Naples, Florida. Her wealth of experience wasn't confined to academies, as she spent 22 years as a private mental performance consultant working with professional athletes and aspiring pros. In addition to her practical work, Eva also imparts her knowledge and wisdom as a professor, mastering in sports psychology and specializing in teaching tennis psychology. Her unique blend of on-court experience and deep insights into the psychology of sport makes her an invaluable asset to both the tennis world and the field of sports psychology. Eva Boris is truly an exemplar of the synergy between athleticism and the power of the mind. Today, Eva presents to us on the Sports Psychology for Match Performance. Over to you Eva. Welcome to my presentation. My name is Eva Boris, I'm a sports psychologist. Before starting, I would like to thank Tennis Australia for my invitation,

because it has been a big pleasure for me to be part of that conference. The topic that I'm going to be talking today is called Tennis a Safe Place to Change. When I was thinking about preparing that conference, I was thinking about the topic of change, how I'm finding every day in my daily work that change. And I was thinking about players that have been working lately, and for example, actually two days ago, a player was telling me, Eva, I was going to prepare a match, but I couldn't warm up. And I said, why you couldn't warm up? And I said, no, because they changed the courts, and the courts that they were for warm up, they were not ready, and I couldn't warm up, and then I started my match, and it was short sets, and I started super cold, and yeah, I lost, and then affected to my second match, it was the backdrop. That was one, for example. Another one, like, was there a day also, a college player? Like, I don't know if you know how it works, but first they played doubles, and after they played singles, she was telling me they changed the line-up with the player that we just finished the doubles, and we just were going to start the singles, and they changed the line-up in the last two minutes, and the plan and everything that was ready to play against that player, I couldn't adapt, I couldn't change, then it took me a set to think about how to deal with that circumstance, and I couldn't, and I couldn't, and affected to my second set,

and I lost the match. Too many times I see players also, like, they are used to travel with some coach, and for whatever reason, the club or the academy, they are telling them, oh, you are going to travel with another one, and they are not ready to accept those changes, they are not ready to travel maybe with another coach, or, yeah, not even to a big, a long tournament, a short tournament that maybe is two hours close by the club, and all those situations that you see with players at different ages, and it's not connected with intelligence or anything, you can see some players that they adapt much better to that, see some situations and there are players like, it is really difficult for them, they get stuck, they don't know how to deal, and instead of accepting those changes that are happening in the tennis life, that there are like a lot, instead of accepting that there are challenges, they accept them as, they take them as threats, and they accept them, that is affecting them to confidence, is affecting them to sustain, and they don't know how to deal, and maybe there are players that there are great, great students in school, there are players like they have incredible capacities, but they don't know how to adapt to that. Those examples with changing coach, with when it's windy, when they have to change the racket, when they have to change the course from indoor to outdoor,

there tennis is a big place of dealing with changes, that can be also a safe place, as it says, the topic of my presentation can be a safe place, where as coaches and educators that we are, we can develop that skill, that are going to help them not just to be a better tennis player, but players that, of course, is going to help them to be a better people, better people with better self-esteem, better confidence, better capacity to deal with the things that are happening in life. And that's the reason that we have, I think, all the people that we are working around, around young players, young kids, that I think we have a huge responsibility to learn, to prepare, to educate the players, how to develop better that fantastic skill that is to change, and also is called too many times resiliency. And that's the topic of my presentation, it's called tennis as a safe place to change. I'm going to pay attention, I'm going to pay attention mostly in young players, like around 8 to 12 years old, because I think in those agencies when the kids are developing the most, is when the kids are, we can create a good structure, pillars like are going to help them in the 14, 13, 15 years old to have a better strength to be dealing with the next challenges that they are facing. Then that's my purpose of today, focusing in early years, for major formation years, like I'm working with a lot with them.
